description: This property lists all test templates that do not complete in any branches of this test run. If there is a template that never successfully completes, this property will fail.
name: All commands were run to completion at least once

description: This property lists all test templates that are not started in any of the branches of this test run.
name: All commands were started at least once

description: This group collects test properties defined with the [Antithesis SDK's](https://antithesis.com/docs/using_antithesis/sdk/) assert.AlwaysOrUnreachable methods. An AlwaysOrUnreachable assertion is one that may or may not be hit on any test run, but that must evaluate to true every time it is hit.
name: Always: Always

description:
This metric tracks the peak memory usage of your software over each test run. The memory used by your software goes up and down as the tests run, and may be different in the different possible histories that were explored by Antithesis, but this metric just tracks the high-water mark across all of those situations.

The value of this metric is a number between 0.0 and 1.0 representing what fraction of the total memory available to the system was being used by your program at the moment of peak usage. If that number goes above 0.95, this property will be marked as 'Failed', because it likely indicates that Antithesis discovered a memory leak or a way to make your application use unbounded memory. This could cause crashes or instability in production, or could be used in a DDOS attack by malicious actors.

The details section for each example will contain information about which processes were using the most memory in the system. The format of this information may change in the future.
name: Always: Peak memory usage

description: This group collects test properties defined with the [Antithesis SDK's](https://antithesis.com/docs/using_antithesis/sdk/) assert.Unreachable method. An unreachability assertion must never be hit on a test run, and will report a failure if it is ever reached. It's semantically equivalent to assert.Always(false), to mark cases that you believe should be impossible to reach.
name: Always: Unreachable

description:
This property reports the unique containers that sent traffic over the Antithesis platform's network bridge. Each example lists a container name for which we saw traffic at some point. This represents a union aggregation across all branches of history, so if a container was seen only in some test paths, it will still be listed here.

You should make sure that all of the containers listed in your Docker Compose or Kubernetes configuration appear here. Containers missing from this list could indicate a misconfigured network, or a container that is failing to start up.
name: Containers joined the Antithesis network

description:
In production, it's tempting to leave excessively verbose logging on all the time, because an issue might only be seen rarely, and could be impossible to reproduce on demand. Since all issues found within the Antithesis platform are perfectly and deterministically reproducible, we recommend running with a moderate level of logging, and dynamically enabling verbose logs when an issue is found.

This property tracks the ratio of logging output to total CPU time spent running the simulation. We recommend keeping this ratio below 200MB/core-hour for best performance of the Antithesis platform. See our [optimization guide](https://antithesis.com/docs/best_practices/optimizing#avoid-excessive-output) for instructions on limiting your logging.
name: Customer output volume

description: This property will fail if the Antithesis instrumentor found paths with more symlinks than were allowed. It lists the invalid paths the Antithesis instrumentor discovered by the container name, the directory it was searching and language.
name: Invalid paths found during Antithesis instrumention

description: This property lists invalid commands discovered by Antithesis. Note that only the first 5 invalid commands will be displayed.
name: Never: Invalid commands found

description: This property aggregates all errors from the Antithesis build step. Failures of this property could be due to misconfiguration of your test, or could reflect a bug in Antithesis itself!
name: No Antithesis build errors

description: This property aggregates all warnings from the Antithesis build step. Failures of this property could be due to misconfiguration of your test, or could reflect a bug in Antithesis itself!
name: No Antithesis build warnings

description: This property aggregates all errors from Antithesis system components and Antithesis SDKs that run within your test environment. Failures of this property could represent misconfiguration of your system, an error reported by an Antithesis SDK in your code, or a bug in Antithesis itself!
name: No Antithesis errors

description: This property aggregates all errors from the Antithesis SaaS service. Failures of this property could be due to misconfiguration of your test, or could reflect a bug in Antithesis itself!
name: No Antithesis session errors

description:
This property tracks containers that exited with codes indicating an error. Containers that exit normally (exit code 0) will not trip this property. Nor will containers exiting with codes 137 and 143, which correspond to SIGKILL and SIGTERM on the container process. This is because attempts to shut down containers with standard tools may generate these codes.

To avoid false positives, please ensure that the main process running within each of your containers exits with code 0 when terminating without error.
name: No unexpected container exits

description:
This property tracks any time a process within the simulation died with a program error signal (for instance SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, etc.). Any such event likely indicates a serious security or reliability issue. In addition to gathering any logs associated with the event, Antithesis will also attempt to provide a core dump from the moment of the crash.

There are rare software systems for which crashing is expected behavior, such as [crash-only software](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/hotos03/tech/full_papers/candea/candea.pdf). If your programs are expected to crash, this property will sometimes generate false positives. In this case, please tell us the names of the programs that are expected to crash, and we will configure your tests so that crashes of those programs do not trigger this property. For each such program, we will also generate a [Sometimes Assertion](https://antithesis.com/docs/best_practices/sometimes_assertions) stating that we should sometimes see it crash.

This property will also catch crashes of Antithesis tools that conduct the testing and run as part of the simulation. If that happens, it's a bug in our software. Please send us the details so we can fix it!
name: No unexpected crashes

description: This property lists the valid paths the Antithesis instrumentor discovered by the container name, the directory it was searching, and language.
name: Paths found for Antithesis instrumentation

description: This property verifies that all images in the environment are built for the expected platform, 'amd64'. You can verify images locally by running `docker inspect [IMAGE] --format {{.Architecture}}`.
name: Software images match expected platform

description: This group collects test properties defined with the [Antithesis SDK's](https://antithesis.com/docs/using_antithesis/sdk/) assert.Reachable method. A reachability assertion must be hit at least once on every test run, and will report a failure if it is never reached. It's semantically equivalent to assert.Sometimes(true), and you can use it like a manually designated bit of code coverage information.
name: Sometimes: Reachable

description: This property lists binaries provided for symbolization whose symbol catalog could not be extracted in full during the environment build, with the reason: not coverage-instrumented at all, a catalog missing some instrumented locations, or a catalog without source locations (usually a build without debug info). Coverage from these binaries still guides testing, but the affected functions will appear as raw addresses or bare names in reports.
name: Symbols were extracted from every binary provided for symbolization

description:
Antithesis uses many VMs running in parallel to efficiently explore a large number of system states. These VMs share physical resources (such as memory) whenever possible.

Sometimes conditions in the system under test cause so much memory pressure that it is impossible to maintain active simultaneous simulation across all of the available VMs. In such situations, Antithesis incrementally reduces parallelism to match its resource constraints. Reducing active VM parallelism is both a last resort and a sign that the workload may be using far more memory than intended (e.g. by generating repeated core dumps).

See the [Antithesis optimization guide](https://antithesis.com/docs/best_practices/optimizing/) for information on how to improve your test efficiency.
name: Test ran with full parallelism

description: This property confirms that the Antithesis fault injector was started.
name: The Antithesis Fault Injector was started

description:
Virtual time per wall time is an important metric of test performance. It tracks the average number of seconds that pass in the simulation for each second of real world time used to run it. This metric is normalized as if we were running on a single-core machine.

Often this number will be lower than 1, because you're running a large number of services inside Antithesis. We are using a single computer to simulate an interacting cluster of computers, so the more "virtual" computers there are, the more work there is for the "real" computer to do, and the slower the tests will run in relative terms.

But a highly-optimized test can actually run faster than realtime! This is because Antithesis technology allows us to "fast-forward" the simulation whenever the software we're testing is idle. For especially well-optimized tests, this effect can cause this metric to go above 1.

If the value of this metric, multiplied by the total number of containers/services you are running, is under 1, then you are likely experiencing a performance problem. Sudden jumps in this metric, either upwards or downwards, can also indicate test misconfiguration (for example a service is not starting up correctly, or going into a busy loop).

See our [optimization guide](http://www.antithesis.com/docs/best_practices/optimizing/#monitor-simulation-efficiency) for more information on improving your simulation efficiency.
name: Virtual time per wall time
